name: Museo Nacional de la Música
funding: National museum listed among the institutions of the Cuban Music Institute, a Ministry of Culture body created in 1989. Founded 1971; its collections grew through musicians' donations.
watch: The Odilio Urfé library and archive merged into the museum in 1997. The library joined IAML in 1995 and IASA in 1999.
records_note: An Instituto Cubano de la Música museum; its site, archived 2013 to 2023, covered collections, services and newsletters.
affiliations_note: Institution of the Cuban Music Institute. Houses the Odilio Urfé library and archive, a member of the International Association of Music Libraries.

overview: Museum of Cuban musical history and instruments in a mansion at Calle Capdevila 1, between Habana and Aguiar, at the entrance to Old Havana (EcuRed; Spanish Wikipedia).

Founded in 1971: EcuRed gives 9 September 1971 and says the first donation, two guitars and decorations of the troubadour María Teresa Vera, reached it that year in a room of the Museo Colonial. The IAML directory also dates the museum to 1971. EcuRed says a restoration of the mansion in 1981 settled the museum there. Spanish Wikipedia dates that restoration to 1971.

Building: the businessman Francisco Pons y Seguí, born in Mahón and a US citizen, bought the plots in 1904. Architect Francisco Ramírez y Ovando finished the house in 1907, and the government bought it in 1936 for the Secretariat of State (Spanish Wikipedia).

Ten rooms, five permanent: mechanical instruments, Afro-Cuban instruments, Cuban ensembles, organology, and a room with pieces of the musician Hubert de Blanck. It holds the original manuscript of the Cuban national anthem by Pedro Figueredo (Spanish Wikipedia).
The Odilio Urfé library and archive, founded in 1949 by the musicologist Odilio Urfé, merged with the museum in 1997 (IAML directory). A 2022 Sul Ponticello piece dates the merger to 1998.
The library says it holds over 140,000 items and joined IAML in 1995 and IASA in 1999 (IAML directory).
details.funding_verdict: Museo Nacional de la Música: mainly public: Cuban Music Institute, Ministry of Culture
funding: EcuRed lists the museum among the institutions of the Cuban Music Institute, which it describes as a Ministry of Culture body created on 11 March 1989.
Collections grew through donations and deposits from musicians and private collectors. The library says it also buys documents from institutions and individuals (IAML directory; Spanish Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The museum's money is Cuban state money through the Ministry of Culture's Music Institute, and no flagged funder was found in the sources opened. The sources give different dates: 1971 (EcuRed, IAML directory, Spanish Wikipedia) or 1981 (EcuRed) for the museum's settling in the mansion, and 1997 (IAML directory) or 1998 (Sul Ponticello) for the archive merger. Worth watching: who funds the library's purchases of documents.

name: Museo Romántico de Trinidad
funding: Open as a museum since 1974, the Palacio Brunet is an 1808 mansion restored from 1964. The Sancti Spíritus heritage centre's 2024 summer programme includes this state museum.
watch: The Asociación Pro Trinidad bought the palace in 1945. Trinidad's historic centre has been on the UNESCO list since 1988.
records_note: In the Sancti Spíritus heritage network; its director told Escambray in 2024 it has no funding for repairs or acquisitions despite yearly takings.
affiliations_note: One of the museums around Trinidad's Plaza Mayor, inside the UNESCO-listed historic centre. Named in the Sancti Spíritus Centro Provincial de Patrimonio's 2024 summer programme (Prensa Latina). Won the 2024 Museo del Año prize from ICOM's Cuban committee and the Consejo Nacional de Patrimonio Cultural.

overview: Museum in the Palacio Brunet on Plaza Mayor, in Trinidad's historic centre, Sancti Spíritus province. The centre has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1988 (Wikipedia, Prensa Latina).

Wikipedia dates the ground floor to 1740 and the upper floor to 1808, built for José Mariano Borrell y Padrón. It passed to his daughter Ángela Borrell y Lemus, Countess of Brunet, whose family kept it until 1857. The Asociación Pro Trinidad bought it in 1945 and full restoration began in 1964.
Opened as the Museo Romántico in 1974 (Wikipedia, Escambray).

Escambray reports about 2,000 pieces, around 900 on show, in four sections: decorative arts, painting and drawing, sculpture and prints, with furniture, porcelain and glass from European makers such as Bohemia, Baccarat and Sèvres.
It received the 2024 Museo del Año prize from the Cuban committee of the International Council of Museums and the Consejo Nacional de Patrimonio Cultural (Escambray).
Visiting: Wikipedia lists opening hours of 8:30 to 17:45, Tuesday to Saturday.
details.funding_verdict: Museo Romántico de Trinidad: mainly public: Ministry of Culture heritage bodies, with its own revenue
funding: Prensa Latina's report on the Sancti Spíritus Centro Provincial de Patrimonio's 2024 summer programme includes this museum. The national heritage council, part of the Ministry of Culture, works through provincial centres to which museums are attached (heritage council site, archived 24 July 2024).

Escambray, 2024: the museum has always had support for its conservation, which the article ties to political will, but despite the revenue it raises each year has no financing for structural repairs or new acquisitions; the article puts this in its paragraph on director Isabel Rueda. Carlos Enrique Sotolongo Peña, who says he started at the museum in April 1990, names the work needed: the false ceiling, the murals and two roof beams.
details.bottom_line: The museum sits in the Ministry of Culture's heritage system, and no flagged funder was found. The weak point, reported by Escambray from the museum, is no dedicated money for repairs or acquisitions. Worth watching: restoration of the ceiling, murals and roof beams, and any published revenue figures.

name: Taller Experimental de Gráfica de La Habana
funding: Print workshop founded 30 July 1962 and listed by the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP) among its institutions in 2013. It earns from print sales and commissions.
watch: Moved to Callejón del Chorro in the 1990s; it has had nine directors since 1962, the latest Yamilys Brito (OnCuba, 2022).
records_note: The CNAP's 2013 page describes a print workshop that sells prints and commissions, naming only its director, Luis Ramón Lara Calaña.
affiliations_note: Listed in 2013 among the institutions of the National Council of Plastic Arts (CNAP); hosts the practical engraving course of Cuba's art schools.

overview: Printmaking workshop in a former warehouse at Callejón del Chorro 62, beside the Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana (OnCuba).

Founded on 30 July 1962 in a small space on the Plaza de la Catedral that shared a portico with the Palacio del Conde de Lombillo. The muralist Orlando Suárez was its first director. Its presses and stones came from the Compañía Litográfica Cubana, a firm that printed labels for the tobacco industry (OnCuba). EcuRed adds that the Chilean painter José Venturelli helped start it and that it was nicknamed the Taller de la Plaza.
It moved to its current building in the 1990s (OnCuba; EcuRed).
Nine directors since 1962, the latest Yamilys Brito Jorge (OnCuba, 2022). ACN quoted her as director in 2025.

Offers courses and runs a gallery that shows and sells works by its masters and graduates. It takes commissions for decoration, custom cards and reproductions, and hosts the practical engraving course of Cuba's art schools (CNAP, 2013).

For its 60th anniversary, the show "Dissonances, marges, fissures", with works by 67 Cuban artists, opened on 2022-11-24 at the University of Western Brittany in Brest, France, with a tour of northern France planned (OnCuba).
details.funding_verdict: Taller Experimental de Gráfica: earns from print sales and commissions; listed in 2013 by CNAP, a Ministry of Culture body
funding: CNAP's 2013 page lists the workshop among its institutions and describes the sales gallery, commissions and cards (CNAP, archive copy of 2013-05-11).
CNAP's institutions page of December 2023 names its member institutions and the workshop is not among them.
details.bottom_line: The workshop sells prints and takes commissions (CNAP, 2013), and CNAP, a Ministry of Culture body, listed it in 2013. The weak point is that CNAP's 2023 institutions page no longer lists the workshop, so the link to the ministry rests on the 2013 page. Worth watching: whether CNAP still counts it among its institutions.

name: Teatro Nacional de Cuba
funding: State theatre run by the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas under the Ministry of Culture. Built from 1951 and opened in 1979; its two halls seat 2,254 and 805.
watch: Its Sala Avellaneda hosted the opening concert of the 41st Jazz Plaza festival in January 2026.
records_note: EcuRed lists the theatre among the council's institutions.
affiliations_note: Part of the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas, with the Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso and the Teatro Julio Antonio Mella.

overview: Theatre complex facing the Plaza de la Revolución in Vedado, Havana (Spanish Wikipedia).
Construction was approved in 1951 under President Carlos Prío Socarrás and the first stone was laid on 29 July 1952 (Spanish Wikipedia). Havana Times says Fulgencio Batista laid it.
The Sala Covarrubias opened in 1960, and the whole complex was inaugurated on 3 September 1979 with a gala for delegates to the Sixth Non-Aligned Movement summit (Spanish Wikipedia).
It has two halls: the Sala Avellaneda, named for the writer Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda, and the smaller Sala Covarrubias, named for the actor Francisco Covarrubias (Spanish Wikipedia).
The Spanish Wikipedia data box gives 2,254 seats for Avellaneda and 805 for Covarrubias. Havana Times also gives 2,254 for Avellaneda, while the Wikipedia text says 3,500 combined.
The original plan took Radio City Music Hall in New York as its model and called for three halls (Spanish Wikipedia).
Avellaneda Hall was set to reopen on 28 October 2012, after a renovation, for the opening of the Havana International Ballet Festival (Havana Times).

The Ballet Nacional de Cuba staged The Nutcracker there in December 2024 (the company's archived site), and the hall hosted the opening concert of the 41st Jazz Plaza festival in January 2026 (EcuRed).
details.funding_verdict: Teatro Nacional de Cuba: state-funded: Ministry of Culture through the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas
funding: EcuRed lists the theatre among the institutions of the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas, and lists that council in the Ministry of Culture's system.

Havana Times reported a 2012 renovation of Avellaneda Hall: all glass panels and lighting fixtures on the façade replaced, the marble polished, and all seats replaced, according to a renovation worker it quoted.

press.overall: Two Havana Times articles cover the building: a 2023 report in which musicians criticise the state's upkeep, and a 2012 report on its renovation.

items.title: Juan Diego Rodriguez (14ymedio), "Electrocution Risk from Leaks at Havana's National Theater" (2023)
points: Reports leaks that flooded the stage of Avellaneda Hall during a Cuban National Ballet performance in March 2023, with water near electrical equipment; the show continued.

Musicians quoted say the building is overrun with termites, that Covarrubias Hall has bats and termites, and that the National Symphony Orchestra's only harp is at risk. A flutist blames corruption and inefficiency in what he calls a failed system.
Unverified: a bassoonist says he was ordered not to reveal the complaints on social media; the article does not say who gave the order.
Says 14ymedio saw a worker on the roof afterwards, and that official media had just published a report acknowledging inefficiency and corruption at state cultural bodies.

items.title: Isbel Diaz Torres, "Cuba's National Theater Completely Restored" (2012)
points: Reports the renovation of Avellaneda Hall before the 23rd Havana ballet festival; the critic Elvis Fuentes calls the removed kinetic sculpture by Osneldo García anachronistic where it stood and says no account of the project was made.
Criticises a placement decision, not the institution.

details.bottom_line: This is a state theatre paid by the Ministry of Culture through the Consejo Nacional de las Artes Escénicas. The weak points are the leaks and termite damage that musicians described in 2023.

name: Unión de Escritores y Artistas de Cuba (UNEAC)
funding: Membership union founded in 1961 that runs galleries, magazines and the Premios Caracol, given since 1978. Its 2020 statutes list dues, a state contribution and donations as income.
watch: UNEAC expelled historian Alina Bárbara López on 12 September 2024 for criticising Revolution leaders. Writer Jorge Fernández Era quit in solidarity before 18 September.
why_flagged: Membership union founded in 1961 that runs galleries, magazines and the Premios Caracol, given since 1978. Its 2020 statutes list dues, a state contribution and donations as income.
records_note: UNEAC's site posts its 2020 statutes, which name its income sources and give no amounts.
affiliations_note: Five national associations (performing artists, visual artists, writers, musicians, and film, radio and television makers) and 14 provincial committees. The Premios Caracol cover film, radio, television and criticism.

overview: Membership union of Cuban writers and artists, based in Havana, with 14 provincial committees (UNEAC site).
Founded on 22 August 1961 by the poet Nicolás Guillén. Alejo Carpentier, José Lezama Lima and René Portocarrero served in its leadership (UNEAC site).
Its 2020 statutes define it as a social organisation with cultural aims and recognise the Communist Party of Cuba as the superior leading force of society and the state (articles 1 and 2).

Stated by the union: it holds special consultative status at the UN Economic and Social Council (UNEAC site), and article 8 of its statutes lists among its objectives to reject and combat any activity contrary to the principles of the Cuban Revolution.
Runs galleries, including the Villa Manuela gallery (UNEAC site). Wikipedia says it has issued the magazine La Gaceta de Cuba since 1962 and given the Caracol awards since 1978.
The site's executive page, archived 18 February 2026, lists Marta Bonet de la Cruz as president. 14ymedio named Luis Morlote as head in 2024.
details.funding_verdict: UNEAC: membership union: dues, a state contribution and donations
funding: Article 81 of the 2020 statutes lists the union's assets: members' dues, a state contribution, donations and bequests, property it owns, artworks held in its buildings, and other income allowed to social organisations, including proceeds of its own art-market activity.
Article 83 puts its economic management under national rules; article 85 lets its National Council, Presidency and Secretariat order audits and inspections of its economic operations.

red_flags.heading: State censorship or punishment
points: 12 September 2024: UNEAC expelled the historian Alina Bárbara López. She says officials of the union, including its president, read her the decision at a meeting of its Matanzas provincial committee, citing article 40 of its regulation (14ymedio). PEN International gives the grounds as activities against the revolution and solidarity with the 11 July movement.

14ymedio adds that the grounds included criticism of Revolution leaders and offending Julio César Pérez, a Communist Party official who is also vice president of the writers' association; López says she received no written decision.
Unverified: López says State Security agents rather than writers and artists dictated the decision (14ymedio, an independent outlet critical of the government).
14 September 2024: the writer Jorge Fernández Era resigned from UNEAC in protest, writing that the union had done nothing about the harassment he and López faced over two years (14ymedio).
14ymedio states that the union has used expulsions as a political tool since 1961 and names Guillermo Cabrera Infante in 1967, Rafael Vilches and Pedro Armando Junco.

press.overall: The coverage opened is news reporting on the 2024 expulsion, from an independent outlet critical of the government.

items.title: "Expulsan a Alina Bárbara López de la Uneac por criticar a la 'alta dirigencia de la Revolución'" (2024)
points: Reports the expulsion and López's reply: the decision was verbal, statutes cannot override the Constitution's guarantee of free expression (article 56), and the union decides without legal argument.
Names UNEAC, its president Luis Morlote and the Party official Julio César Pérez.

items.title: "Jorge Fernández Era renuncia a la Uneac en solidaridad con Alina Bárbara López" (2024)
points: Reports Fernández Era's letter to the UNEAC presidency, which says the union ignored the legal complaints he and López filed.
Names UNEAC and its presidency.

wider_context: PEN International, an advocacy group, records that López was detained in April 2024 and for 11 hours on 18 June 2024, and charged under article 182 of the Penal Code with attempted assault on police officers (three to eight years). PEN holds that the charge was brought to limit her critical activity.
The police, not UNEAC, carried out the detentions. UNEAC expelled her on 12 September 2024, after both events.
details.bottom_line: Income comes from dues, a state contribution and donations, and no flagged funder was found. The weak point is documented: the union itself expelled López on 12 September 2024, under statutes that recognise the Communist Party as the superior leading force of society and the state. Worth watching: written grounds and appeals for future sanctions, and any published accounts.

name: Villa Rothmayer
funding: Run by the Museum of Prague, which the City of Prague funds with a CZK 227.9M subsidy (2024). The museum site also names the Education Ministry and Erasmus as supporters.
watch: Architect Otto Rothmayer's own villa of 1929 in Prague 6, with 3,558 visitors in 2024. Its garden opened free to the public in May 2026.
records_note: Covered by the Museum of Prague's 2024 report, which lists the villa's visitors and the city subsidy.
finances_note: Museum-wide 2024 (annual report): city subsidy CZK 227.9M, revenue besides the subsidy CZK 23.1M, costs CZK 254.9M. The villa had 3,558 visitors.
affiliations_note: Run by the Museum of Prague, a municipal contributory organisation of the City of Prague, together with Villa Müller. Member of Iconic Houses (house page on iconichouses.org and the museum's report).

overview: Family home of the architect Otto Rothmayer at U Páté baterie 896/50 in Prague 6, on the border of Břevnov and Střešovice near the Central Military Hospital (Museum of Prague, Expats.cz).
Rothmayer built it in 1928 to 1929 from concepts by Jože Plečnik, whose student and collaborator he was at Prague Castle and Lány Castle. The villa is named for him (Expats.cz).
His wife, the textile artist Božena Rothmayerová, had her study there. The spiral staircase carries artefacts he brought home from Prague Castle (Museum of Prague).
The garden holds glass sculptures by René and Miluše Roubíček. The photographer Josef Sudek, a friend of Rothmayer, drew on it for his "Magic Garden" series (Expats.cz).

Expats.cz reported on 2026-05-28 that the Museum of Prague had opened the garden free to the public on Tuesdays, Thursdays and weekends. The museum's visit page still says the garden is closed in winter and otherwise open only on guided tours.

Visiting: tours Wednesday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday 10:00 to 16:00 and Thursday 12:00 to 18:00, every two hours, with prior reservation. Tickets cost CZK 250, or CZK 180 reduced. The villa had 3,558 visitors in 2024 (Museum of Prague, annual report 2024).
details.funding_verdict: Villa Rothmayer: mainly public: the City of Prague through the Museum of Prague
funding: In 2024 the museum received a non-investment contribution of CZK 227,913.4 thousand (annual report 2024; the report does not name the payer, which the atlas record gives as the City of Prague).

The museum's front page shows seven partner logos under "Who makes my Museum possible", named only by image file: the City of Prague, Czech Radio, Czech Television, Erasmus, the Association of Museums and Galleries, the Education Ministry and Kudy z nudy.
details.bottom_line: City money through one museum pays for the villa; no flagged funder appears, and no villa-only figures were found. Worth watching: the cost and payer of the 2026 garden opening are not stated.

name: Museo de Arte Moderno de Santo Domingo
funding: State museum run by the Dominican Ministry of Culture on the Plaza de la Cultura; its director sits on the ministry's Bienal Nacional commission.
watch: In November 2025, 155 signatories asked the ministry to restore the jury's award at the 31st Bienal, held here. Earlier letters: 2020, 2021.
why_flagged: State museum run by the Dominican Ministry of Culture on the Plaza de la Cultura; its director sits on the ministry's Bienal Nacional commission.
records_note: It posts nothing itself; its parent Ministry of Culture posts annual memorias for 2016 to 2025 and financial statements for 2020 to 2025.
affiliations_note: The museum is attached to the Dirección General de Museos and the Ministry of Culture, like seven other Santo Domingo state museums.

overview: State modern art museum in the Plaza de la Cultura Juan Pablo Duarte complex, Santo Domingo (El Día, 2016).
Opened on 15 December 1976 (El Día, 2016).
Designed by architect José Miniño. A concrete building with three levels and a basement (El Día; El Inmobiliario, 2022).
Remodelled for about four years and reopened during the COVID-19 pandemic. Holds more than 1,500 pieces, 80 to 100 shown at a time (El Inmobiliario, 2022).
Hosts the Bienal Nacional de Artes Visuales. The 2025 edition showed 207 works chosen from 609 registered, at the museum (Acento, José Rafael Sosa, 2025).
Began as the Galería de Arte Moderno in 1976 and was renamed in 1992 (El Inmobiliario). Open Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 18:00 with free admission, as reported in October 2022 (El Inmobiliario).
details.funding_verdict: Museo de Arte Moderno de Santo Domingo: public: Dominican Ministry of Culture
funding: The Ministry of Culture has overseen the museum since 2000 (El Inmobiliario, 2022). Artists' open letters hold the Ministry of Culture and the museum jointly responsible for the Bienal (El Nuevo Diario, 2020; Diario Libre, 2021).
Museum director Federico Fondeur and curator Ana A. Fernández sit on the organising commission for the XXX Bienal, sworn in by Culture Minister Milagros Germán (El Día, 25 October 2022).

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: Postponement: the Ministry postponed the opening of the 29th Bienal on 16 December 2019, one day before the scheduled date, saying renovations at the museum were unfinished (Diario Libre, 16 December 2019; El Nuevo Diario, 16 July 2020).
Protest: the Comité de la Bienal Invisible called a protest at the Plaza de la Cultura on 17 December 2019 at 5:30 p.m., demanding that the biennials be held on schedule (Diario Libre).

July 2020 letter: La Bienal Invisible, La Otra Bienal and La Cooperativa called the handling of the 29th Bienal negligent, blaming the Ministry and the museum; the 25 signers included Guadalupe Casasnovas and Raquel Paiewonsky. They said works submitted for the 29th edition had been kept at the museum for nearly two years without explanation, and named Minister Eduardo Selman and María Elena Ditrén, who it says had directed the museum for 16 years (El Nuevo Diario, 16 July 2020).

June 2021 letter: more than 60 artists, curators and other cultural workers signed a letter dated 11 June 2021 denouncing the "deficiente manejo" of the 29th Bienal, saying the selection list included works withdrawn before selection. They named Minister Carmen Heredia and museum director Federico Fondeur (Diario Libre, 23 June 2021).
2025: the lack of published catalogues for the 2021 and 2023 Bienales drew criticism, and artist Ramón Peña said he would no longer take part (Acento, 9 September 2025).

press.overall: Criticism is frequent but comes from newspapers and artists' collectives, not art press. It concerns the Bienal's management and the Ministry, more than the museum's collection.

items.title: "Artistas califican de negligencia la no celebración de la Bienal Nacional de Artes Visuales" (2020)
points: Artists say the Bienal was effectively cancelled, not postponed, and ask for a Bienal independent of any single building, run by a permanent management committee.
Names the Ministry of Culture and the museum; 25 signatories.

items.title: "Más de 60 artistas denuncian 'deficiente manejo' de 29 Bienal de Artes Visuales" (2021)
points: The letter says state cultural institutions "carecen de voluntad política" to take responsibility to the artistic community. The article carries no reply from the Ministry or the museum.

items.title: José Rafael Sosa, "Bienales de Artes Visuales de Santo Domingo, o el cuento de nunca acabar" (2025)
points: Lists recurring complaints about the Bienales since 1998 and asks whether a 2025 prize for a potted palm should follow the jury's ruling or article 8 of the competition rules, which excludes perishable materials.
Names the jury (Raúl Morilla, Lillian Carrasco, Hiromi Shiba); the museum is the venue and is not the main target.

details.bottom_line: The museum is a state institution with no private sponsor named, so the money is not the issue. The weak points are the repeated delays and Bienal management that artists blamed on the Ministry and the museum in 2019, 2020 and 2021, and the lack of published budget or catalogue information. Worth watching: whether the permanent Bienal committee that artists asked for in 2020 is created and publishes accounts.

name: 6th of October War Panorama
funding: Egypt's state commissioned it under President Mubarak and the National Military Museums Department runs it. North Korean architects helped build it; tickets cost 3 to 30 Egyptian pounds in 2010.
watch: Opened 5 October 1989. Public Delivery names Mansudae Overseas Projects as co-builder.
records_note: Egypt Independent (October 2010) gives the ticket prices.
affiliations_note: Run by the Egyptian National Military Museums Department.

propaganda.summary: Conceived by Hosni Mubarak after a North Korea visit, built by North Korean artists and opened 5 October 1989. Run by the Egyptian military, it presents the 1973 war as unbroken victory.

overview: War museum and memorial to the 1973 October War in Heliopolis, Cairo, on Salah Salem Street. It covers 7.5 feddans, about 32,000 square metres (Wikipedia; Egypt Independent).
Inaugurated on 5 October 1989 by President Hosni Mubarak (Wikipedia).
A cylindrical, fort-like building in Islamic architectural style. Wikipedia says a group of North Korean architects gave partial assistance. Egypt Independent says Koreans built it over five years.

The visit has three shows: a short documentary, a moving model of the Suez Canal coast, and a 360-degree painted mural on a rotating platform. Tanks, aircraft and guns stand in an outdoor display (Egypt Independent; Wikipedia).
Visiting: in 2010 the panorama was open daily from 9AM to 9PM except Tuesdays. Tickets cost 3 Egyptian pounds for Egyptians, 10 for Arabs and 30 for foreigners (Egypt Independent, 2010).
details.funding_verdict: 6th of October War Panorama: public: the Egyptian state; the National Military Museums Department runs it
funding: President Mubarak commissioned it (Egypt Independent), and the Egyptian National Military Museums Department runs it (Wikipedia; Public Delivery).
North Korean role: Public Delivery names Mansudae Overseas Projects as a collaborator on the build.
not_related: the Tishreen War Panorama, also called the October War Panorama, in Damascus, Syria. It shares the name and North Korean help but is a separate museum run by the Syrian Ministry of Defence (Wikipedia).

press.overall: One visitor review discusses the panorama. It criticises upkeep and presentation, not the funding.

items.title: Ali Abdel Mohsen, "Egypt's Museums II: The October War Panorama" (2010)
points: Calls the panorama marred by incompetence: misspellings on the ticket, war vehicles repainted in one flat green, a documentary too degraded to follow, and kiosks selling toys and trinkets, with celebrity posters for sale inside.
Calls the third show's rotating mural striking and realistic, and concludes the visit offers amusement and frustration but no education.
Mentions North Korea only as "Koreans" who built it over five years.

details.bottom_line: The Egyptian state commissioned and runs the panorama, and no flagged funder was found in the sources opened. Wikipedia and Public Delivery describe the North Korean role as partial assistance and collaboration on the build. Worth watching: the upkeep problems the 2010 review described.

name: Contemporary Image Collective
funding: The Arab Fund for Arts and Culture lists a 2024 CiC project under Egypt's National Cultural Opportunities Fund. Cairo artists depend on foreign grants.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Says a board of trustees exists without naming it.

overview: Independent non-profit arts initiative in Cairo, focused on visual culture, artistic practice and critical discourse (Arab Fund for Arts and Culture; e-flux).
Founded in 2004 in Cairo by a group of visual artists and professional photographers (e-flux; TransArtists).

Earlier sites: a villa in Mounira, then from 2010 an entire floor of a colonial-era apartment building in Downtown Cairo, near Talaat Harb Square (Cairo 360, Aleksandra Sekinger, 23 June 2010). TransArtists lists the address as 22 Abdel Khalek Tharwat, 4th Floor, Downtown.
DutchCulture reported in August 2025 that CiC lost its downtown location and secured a new space in the Garden City district.

Facilities and programme: exhibitions, educational programmes, a library, a workshop space and printing facilities (Arab Fund for Arts and Culture; DutchCulture). TransArtists lists a lighting studio, a darkroom, a digital lab and two multi-purpose rooms.
It has no fixed residency programme and invites artists to occasional residencies within its curated programme (TransArtists).
details.funding_verdict: Contemporary Image Collective: independent non-profit with grant-funded projects
funding: The Arab Fund for Arts and Culture lists Contemporary Image Collective under the National Cultural Opportunities Fund (NCOF), 2024, Egypt, on its supported projects pages.
TransArtists states that CiC seeks funds for all programming it commits to, and that participants in some programmes pay a fee that varies with the programme.
details.bottom_line: Contemporary Image Collective is an independent non-profit arts initiative founded in 2004. The Arab Fund for Arts and Culture lists a 2024 project under the National Cultural Opportunities Fund, and TransArtists states that CiC seeks funds for its programming.

name: Medrar for Contemporary Art
funding: Space set up with support from Young Arab Theatre Fund, Foundation for Arts Initiatives, Abbara, Roberto Cimetta Fund, Netherlands Embassy in Cairo and AFAC through a Swiss SDC grant.
watch: Artist collective since 2005; runs the Cairo Video Festival. AFAC lists a 2019 North Africa Cultural Program grant.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Non-profit art space for contemporary and media arts, at 10 Gamal El Din Abou El Mahasen Street, 8th floor, Garden City, Cairo (Medrar).

Running since 2005. Medrar began as a collective of visual artists working with a new medium, and its first project was the Cairo Video Festival, through which Medrar was later established (Experimental Cinema directory). Medrar's about page describes it as a non-profit art space running since 2005, thanks Dia Hamed as co-founder and lists Mohamed Allam as director.

Projects: the Cairo Video Festival, Medrar Studio, MedRX, Roznama and Medrar TV, plus a collaborative space for media artists, workshops, events and documentation of audio-visual work on Egypt's contemporary art scene (Medrar).

The Cairo Video Festival is a platform for video art with about ten days of screenings, artist talks and discussions (Experimental Cinema directory). The credits of the 9th festival (2019) list Mena El Shazly as artistic director (Cairo Video Festival acknowledgements).
details.funding_verdict: Medrar for Contemporary Art: grant-funded: arts foundations, an embassy and the Arab Fund for Arts and Culture
funding: Medrar's about page thanks as supporters the Young Arab Theatre Fund, the Foundation for Arts Initiatives, Culture Resource's Abbara Program, the Roberto Cimetta Fund, the Netherlands Embassy in Cairo and the Arab Fund for Arts and Culture (AFAC), the last through a grant from the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation.
AFAC lists a 2019 grant to Medrar from its North Africa Cultural Program, aimed at long-term financial stability and wider artistic outreach (AFAC).
details.bottom_line: Medrar is a small independent art space whose documented money comes from arts funds and foundations, one embassy and a Swiss development agency grant passed through AFAC. AFAC lists a 2019 grant from its North Africa Cultural Program.
